title: Graph Data Structure
html:
A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges — the most general way to store pairwise relationships. Road maps, social networks, task dependencies and the web are all graphs, and almost every algorithm here (BFS, DFS, topological sort, Dijkstra, MST) is an interview staple.

Graph — a pair G = (V, E) where V is a finite set of vertices (nodes) and E is a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices. Unlike a tree a graph may contain cycles, may be disconnected, and has no root.

Graph vs tree

TreeGraph
EdgesExactly n − 1 for n nodesAny number, 0 … V(V−1)/2 (undirected)
CyclesNeverAllowed
ConnectedAlwaysMay be disconnected
Root / hierarchyOne root, parent → childNo root; vertices are peers
TraversalPre/in/post-order, level orderBFS / DFS with a visited array (cycles would loop forever)
Key point

A tree is a special case of a graph: a connected, acyclic, undirected graph. Everything that works on graphs works on trees, but tree algorithms rely on the absence of cycles and need visited bookkeeping before they can run on a graph.

Directed and undirected graphs

Directed graph (digraph)Undirected graph
Edge (u, v)Goes from u to v onlyJoins u and v both ways
Degreeindegree(v) = edges into v, outdegree(v) = edges out of vdegree(v) = number of edges touching v
Degree sumΣ indegree = Σ outdegree = |E|Σ degree = 2·|E| (every edge is counted at both ends)
Maximum edges (no self-loops)|V| · (|V| − 1) — every ordered pair|V| · (|V| − 1) / 2 — every unordered pair
ExamplesWeb links, task dependencies, follows on TwitterRoads, friendships, electrical circuits
Undirected: 0 ≤ |E| ≤ |V|(|V|−1)/2 Directed: 0 ≤ |E| ≤ |V|(|V|−1)
Key point

The degree-sum formula (the handshake lemma) gives a quick sanity check: in an undirected graph the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. A graph with |E| close to the maximum is dense; one with |E| ≈ |V| is sparse — the distinction decides between the two representations below.

Walk, path and cycle

In the undirected graph above:

  • Walk — any sequence of vertices where consecutive vertices are adjacent; vertices and edges may repeat: v1, v2, v4, v3, v1, v2.
  • Path — a walk with no repeated vertex: v1, v2, v4.
  • Cycle — a walk that starts and ends at the same vertex (a simple cycle repeats no other vertex): v1, v2, v4, v3, v1.
  • Connected (undirected) — a path exists between every pair of vertices. Strongly connected (directed) — a directed path exists in both directions between every pair.

Cyclic directed

A digraph that contains at least one directed cycle, e.g. A → B → C → A. Topological sort is impossible.

Cyclic undirected

Any undirected graph with a cycle; a graph with more than V − 1 edges is always cyclic.

Undirected acyclic

A forest — each connected component is a tree, exactly V − 1 edges when connected.

Directed acyclic (DAG)

Directed with no cycles: dependency graphs, build systems, course prerequisites. Admits a topological order.

Weighted and unweighted graphs

  • Unweighted — every edge counts as 1. The shortest path is the one with the fewest edges and BFS finds it.
  • Weighted — each edge carries a number. The shortest path minimises the sum of weights: Dijkstra (non-negative weights), Bellman–Ford (negative weights allowed), or a single pass over a topological order (DAGs).
  • Weights can be negative; a negative cycle makes “shortest path” undefined because going round it again always lowers the total.

Representation: adjacency matrix

A V × V matrix with mat[i][j] = 1 (or the weight) when there is an edge from i to j, else 0. An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix; a directed graph does not.

Adjacency matrixCost
SpaceΘ(V²) — even for a graph with very few edges
Is u adjacent to v?Θ(1) — read mat[u][v]
All neighbours of uΘ(V) — scan row u
Degree of uΘ(V) — count the 1s in row u
Add / remove an edgeΘ(1)
Add / remove a vertexΘ(V²) — the whole matrix is rebuilt

Vertices with arbitrary names

Algorithms index arrays by vertex number, but real vertices are cities, user ids or strings. Keep two mappings: a hash map name → index to translate input, and an array index → name (just the list of names) to translate results back. Everything in between runs on plain integers.

Representation: adjacency list

An array of V lists; adj[u] holds the neighbours of u (for a weighted graph, (neighbour, weight) pairs). The lists are usually dynamic arrays (vector, ArrayList, Python list) — linked lists also work but are slower to scan. This is the default representation for every algorithm in these notes.

Adjacency listCost
SpaceΘ(V + E) — V + 2E list entries undirected, V + E directed
Is u adjacent to v?O(degree(u)) — scan adj[u] (O(1) if each list is a hash set)
All neighbours of uΘ(degree(u))
Degree of uΘ(1) — the list length
Add an edgeΘ(1) — append
Remove an edgeO(degree(u)) — find it first

Adjacency list vs adjacency matrix

OperationAdjacency listAdjacency matrix
MemoryΘ(V + E)Θ(V²)
Is there an edge u → v?O(degree(u)), worst O(V)Θ(1)
Visit all neighbours of uΘ(degree(u))Θ(V)
Add an edgeΘ(1)Θ(1)
Remove an edgeO(V)Θ(1)
Whole traversal (BFS / DFS)Θ(V + E)Θ(V²)
Key point

Use the list for sparse graphs (E ≈ V, which is nearly every real graph — a road network or social graph has far fewer than V² edges) and whenever you traverse. Use the matrix for dense graphs, when edge lookups dominate, or for matrix algorithms such as Floyd–Warshall. The matrix also stores redundant information for undirected graphs: both mat[u][v] and mat[v][u].

Breadth First Search (BFS)

BFS explores a graph level by level from a source: first the source, then every vertex one edge away, then two edges away, and so on. A queue holds the frontier; a visited array stops cycles from being walked twice.

Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 2-4, 3-5, 4-5, s = 0
Output: 0 1 2 3 4 5
Input: same graph, s = 2
Output: 2 0 3 4 1 5

Idea

Mark the source visited and enqueue it. Repeatedly dequeue a vertex, output it, and enqueue every unvisited neighbour, marking it visited the moment it is enqueued. Because the queue is FIFO, all vertices at distance d leave the queue before any vertex at distance d + 1 — which is exactly what makes BFS find shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

Marking a vertex visited when it is dequeued instead of when it is enqueued lets the same vertex enter the queue several times (once per neighbour that sees it) — correct output on small graphs, but up to O(E) queue entries and duplicated work on large ones.

BFS on a disconnected graph and counting components

A single BFS only reaches the source's component. To cover a graph that may be disconnected, loop over every vertex and start a new BFS from each one that is still unvisited. Every restart is one more connected component.

Example

Input: edges = 0-2, 2-1, 3-4, 5-7, 5-6, 6-7, V = 8
Output: 3 components: {0,2,1} {3,4} {5,7,6}

Idea

Share one visited array across all the BFS calls. The outer loop for u in 0..V-1 finds the next unvisited vertex; each BFS from it visits exactly its component, so the number of BFS calls equals the number of components.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)

Shortest path in an unweighted graph (BFS distances)

Because BFS visits vertices in order of their distance from the source, the first time it reaches a vertex is along a shortest path. Record dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 and parent[v] = u when v is enqueued from u; following parent backwards from any vertex rebuilds the path.

Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-4, 4-5, 4-6, s = 0
Output: dist = 0 1 1 2 3 4 4, path 0→5 = 0 1 3 4 5

Idea

Initialise every distance to -1 (unreached). The visited array becomes unnecessary: dist[v] == -1 means not yet seen. A vertex that is still -1 after BFS is unreachable from the source.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Key point

This only works when every edge costs the same. With weights, a path with more edges can be cheaper — that is what Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford handle below.

Applications of BFS

Shortest path, unweighted

Fewest hops between two vertices — road hops, degrees of separation, moves in a puzzle.

Web crawlers

Start at a seed page and visit links level by level, so nearby pages are indexed first.

Peer-to-peer networks

Finding neighbouring peers (e.g. BitTorrent) — close nodes are discovered before distant ones.

Social network search

Friends within k hops, friend suggestions: a BFS cut off at depth k.

Garbage collection

Cheney's copying collector is a BFS over live objects starting from the roots.

Cycle detection

In an undirected graph a visited neighbour that is not the parent closes a cycle.

Broadcasting

A message sent to all neighbours, who forward it to theirs — flooding in networks.

Max flow (Edmonds–Karp)

Ford–Fulkerson with BFS to pick the shortest augmenting path each round.

Depth First Search (DFS)

DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking: from the current vertex it recurses into the first unvisited neighbour, and only when that whole branch is exhausted does it try the next neighbour. The recursion stack (or an explicit stack) replaces BFS's queue.

Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 2-4, 3-5, 4-5, s = 0
Output: 0 1 3 2 4 5
Input: same graph, s = 2
Output: 2 0 1 3 5 4

Idea

dfs(u): mark u visited, output it, then dfs(v) for every unvisited neighbour v. The visited check is what prevents an infinite loop on cycles — compare the tree traversals, which need no such check.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V) for visited + recursion stack
Pitfall

Recursive DFS on a long path uses one stack frame per vertex: Python stops at ~1000 frames and Java/C++ crash on graphs with tens of thousands of vertices in a chain. For large inputs convert to an explicit stack — but note that the naive iterative version (push all neighbours, pop one) visits in a different order than the recursive one.

DFS on a disconnected graph and counting components

Exactly as with BFS: an outer loop over all vertices, a shared visited array, and one recursive DFS per unvisited vertex. The number of calls made by the outer loop is the number of connected components.

Example

Input: edges = 0-2, 2-1, 3-4, 5-7, 5-6, 6-7, V = 8
Output: 3 components

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)

Applications of DFS

  • Cycle detection — a back edge to a vertex that is still on the recursion stack (directed) or to a visited non-parent (undirected).
  • Topological sorting — vertices in decreasing order of DFS finish time.
  • Strongly connected components — Kosaraju's and Tarjan's algorithms are two DFS passes, or one DFS with low-link values.
  • Mazes and puzzles — explore one path to the end before trying another; backtracking is DFS over the state space.
  • Path finding — any path (not necessarily shortest) between two vertices; articulation points and bridges via discovery times.
BFSDFS
Data structureQueueStack / recursion
VisitsBy distance (level order)Along one branch, then backtracks
Finds shortest paths (unweighted)YesNo
MemoryO(width) — the frontierO(depth) — the current path
Typical usesShortest path, nearest neighbour, level-wise processingCycles, topological order, SCCs, connectivity, backtracking

Detect a cycle in an undirected graph

Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 1-2, 1-3, 2-3
Output: cycle
Input: edges = 0-1, 1-2, 1-3
Output: no cycle

Idea

Run DFS remembering each vertex's parent (the vertex we came from). Reaching a neighbour that is already visited and is not the parent means there are two different routes to it — a cycle. Without the parent check every undirected edge would look like a cycle, because u → v and v → u are the same edge.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

The parent check breaks down with parallel edges (two edges between the same pair) — they form a cycle, yet the second one looks like the edge we arrived by. Track the parent edge index instead of the parent vertex if the input may contain multi-edges. Shortcut: a connected undirected graph with E ≥ V edges always has a cycle.

Detect a cycle in a directed graph

Example

Input: edges = 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→1
Output: cycle
Input: edges = 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3
Output: no cycle

Idea

In a digraph “visited” is not enough: graph 2 reaches 3 twice (via 1 and via 2) without any cycle. A cycle exists only when DFS reaches a vertex that is still on the recursion stack — an ancestor of the current call. Keep a second array onStack that is set on entry and cleared on exit; a neighbour with onStack[v] true is a back edge.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Key point

The same idea is often written with three colours: white = unvisited, grey = on the recursion stack, black = finished. An edge to a grey vertex is a back edge (cycle); an edge to a black vertex is a cross/forward edge and harmless. Kahn's algorithm below detects directed cycles without recursion.

Topological sort — Kahn's algorithm (BFS)

Topological order — a linear ordering of the vertices of a DAG such that for every edge u → v, u comes before v. It is the order in which tasks with dependencies can be executed. A graph with a cycle has no topological order; a DAG may have several.

Example

Input: edges = 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1, V = 6
Output: 4 5 2 0 3 1 (one valid order; 5 4 2 3 1 0 is another)

Idea

A vertex with indegree 0 has no unfinished prerequisites, so it can go first. Output it, then “delete” it by decrementing the indegree of each neighbour; any neighbour that drops to 0 is now free and joins the queue. Repeat until the queue is empty.

1
Count indegrees
indeg[v] = number of edges into v, one pass over the adjacency lists.
2
Seed the queue
Enqueue every vertex with indeg[v] == 0.
3
Process
Dequeue u, append it to the order; for every neighbour v: indeg[v] -= 1, and enqueue v when it reaches 0.
4
Finish
When the queue is empty the order is complete — if it holds fewer than V vertices, the graph has a cycle (next section).
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Key point

Swap the queue for a min-priority queue and Kahn's algorithm yields the lexicographically smallest topological order — a common follow-up question.

Cycle detection with Kahn's algorithm

Kahn's algorithm only ever outputs vertices whose indegree reached 0. The vertices on a cycle depend on each other, so none of them ever reaches 0 and they are never output. Therefore: fewer than V vertices in the result ⇔ the graph has a cycle. This is the iterative alternative to the recursion-stack method.

Example

Input: edges = 5→2, 5→0, 4→0, 4→1, 2→3, 3→1, V = 6
Output: no cycle
Input: edges = 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, V = 4
Output: cycle

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)

Topological sort using DFS

Idea

When dfs(u) finishes, every vertex reachable from u has already finished (it was either visited inside the call or earlier). So a vertex finishes after all of its descendants — reversing the finish order puts every u before everything it points to. Push each vertex onto a stack as its DFS returns, then pop the stack.

1
Visit every vertex
For u in 0 … V−1: if u is unvisited, call dfs(u) — this covers disconnected DAGs.
2
dfs(u)
Mark u visited, recurse into every unvisited neighbour, and then push u onto the stack (post-order).
3
Read the stack
Pop until empty — the pop order is a topological order.
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

The DFS version silently produces a (wrong) order when the graph has a cycle — it never checks. Either run the directed-cycle check first (onStack) or use Kahn's algorithm, which detects the cycle for free.

Shortest path in a DAG

In a DAG a vertex's distance is final as soon as every vertex that can reach it is settled — and a topological order lists exactly those vertices first. One relaxation pass in topological order therefore gives all shortest paths, even with negative weights, in linear time. No priority queue, no repeated passes.

Example

Input: edges above, s = 0
Output: 0 2 3 6 1 5
Input: s = 1
Output: INF 0 3 9 INF INF

1
Initialise
dist[v] = INF for all v, dist[s] = 0.
2
Topological order
DFS-based (or Kahn's) topological sort of the whole graph.
3
Relax in order
For each u in topological order with dist[u] != INF: for each edge u → v with weight w, if dist[u] + w < dist[v] set dist[v] = dist[u] + w.
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Key point

Negate every weight (or use max instead of min) and the same pass gives the longest path in a DAG — the critical path in project scheduling. Longest path in a general graph is NP-hard; the DAG structure is what makes it easy.

Dijkstra's algorithm

Single-source shortest paths in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It is a greedy BFS: instead of a FIFO queue it always expands the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, so each vertex is settled exactly once, in increasing order of distance.

Example

Input: edges above (undirected), s = 0
Output: dist = 0 3 1 8 10, path 0→4 = 0 2 1 3 4

Idea

Suppose u has the smallest tentative distance among the unsettled vertices. Any other route to u would have to leave the settled set through some unsettled vertex x with dist[x] ≥ dist[u], and with non-negative weights it can only get longer from there — so dist[u] is already optimal. Settle u, relax its edges, repeat. A negative edge breaks the “can only get longer” step, which is why Dijkstra fails with negative weights.

1
Initialise
dist[s] = 0, every other dist[v] = INF; push (0, s) into a min-heap keyed by distance.
2
Extract-min
Pop (d, u). If d > dist[u] it is a stale entry — skip it (lazy deletion).
3
Relax
For every edge u → v with weight w: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] = dist[u] + w, parent[v] = u, and push (dist[v], v).
4
Stop
When the heap is empty every reachable vertex is settled; INF marks the unreachable ones.
Time O((V + E) log V) with a binary heapSpace O(V + E)

The textbook version without a heap scans the whole dist array to find the minimum each round. It is O(V²) — fine for dense graphs or an adjacency matrix, and worth knowing because it is what the heap version optimises:

Pitfall

Negative edge weights break Dijkstra. The algorithm assumes a settled vertex can never be improved; a negative edge discovered later can improve it. With a settled array the result is simply wrong; with the lazy-deletion heap version it may still be right but can re-settle vertices exponentially many times, and a negative cycle makes it loop forever. Use Bellman–Ford instead.

Key point

Does adding a constant to every edge keep the shortest path? No. Path 0→1→2 with weights 1 + 1 = 2 beats the direct edge 0→2 of weight 3; add 2 to every edge and it becomes 6 against 5. Paths with more edges are penalised more, so the shortest path can change — which is why Johnson's algorithm reweights with vertex potentials rather than a constant.

Bellman–Ford algorithm

Single-source shortest paths that allow negative edge weights and detect negative cycles. Instead of picking vertices cleverly it relaxes every edge, V − 1 times. After pass i, every shortest path that uses at most i edges is final; a shortest path has at most V − 1 edges, so V − 1 passes suffice.

Example

Input: edges above, s = 0, V = 5
Output: 0 -1 2 -2 1
Input: same edges plus 3→4 (−1)
Output: negative-weight cycle

Idea

Shortest paths of one edge are found in pass 1, two edges in pass 2, and so on — each pass extends the frontier of correct distances by one edge. If a V-th pass can still improve something, a path with V edges is shorter than every path with fewer edges, which is only possible by going round a negative cycle.

1
Initialise
dist[s] = 0, every other dist[v] = INF.
2
Relax V − 1 times
For every edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] != INF and dist[u] + w < dist[v], set dist[v] = dist[u] + w.
3
Check for a negative cycle
One more pass over all edges — if any edge can still be relaxed, a negative-weight cycle is reachable from s.
Time O(V · E)Space O(V)
BFSDAG passDijkstraBellman–Ford
Weightsnone / all equalany (DAG only)non-negativeany
Negative cycles—impossible in a DAGwrong resultdetected
TimeO(V + E)O(V + E)O((V + E) log V)O(V · E)
Typical usehops, gridsscheduling, DP on DAGsmaps, routingcurrency arbitrage, distance-vector routing (RIP)
Key point

Stop early when a whole pass changes nothing — on most graphs that happens long before V − 1 passes. SPFA (queue-based Bellman–Ford) only re-relaxes edges out of vertices whose distance changed; same worst case, much faster on average.

Strongly connected components — Kosaraju's algorithm

Strongly connected component (SCC) — a maximal set of vertices in a directed graph in which every vertex can reach every other. Collapsing each SCC to a single vertex turns any digraph into a DAG (the condensation).

Example

Input: edges above, V = 7
Output: {0,1,2} {3,4,5} {6} — 3 components

Idea

Reverse every edge and the SCCs stay the same, but the edges between them flip. A DFS on the original graph finishes the “source” SCC last; starting the second DFS there, on the reversed graph, cannot leak into other SCCs (their edges now point towards it), so each DFS of the second pass collects exactly one SCC.

1
DFS and record finish order
Run DFS over the whole graph, pushing each vertex onto a stack as it finishes (the same post-order used for topological sort).
2
Reverse the graph
Build rev with every edge u → v turned into v → u.
3
DFS the reversed graph in stack order
Pop vertices from the stack; for each unvisited one, DFS in rev — every vertex reached is in its SCC.
Time O(V + E)Space O(V + E) for the reversed graph
Key point

Kosaraju emits SCCs in topological order of the condensation (sources first: {0,1,2} before {3,4,5} before {6}); Tarjan's algorithm below emits them in reverse. A digraph is strongly connected exactly when the count is 1.

Strongly connected components — Tarjan's algorithm

One DFS pass instead of two. Every vertex gets a discovery time disc[u] and a low-link low[u]: the smallest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using at most one back edge to a vertex that is still on the stack. A vertex with low[u] == disc[u] is the root of an SCC — everything above it on the stack belongs to that component.

Idea

Keep every vertex on an explicit stack from the moment it is discovered until its SCC is complete. A back edge to a stacked vertex v lowers low[u] to disc[v]; after visiting a child v, low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). If, when u finishes, nothing in its subtree reached anything discovered earlier (low[u] == disc[u]), then u and all vertices stacked after it form one SCC — pop them off.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

For the back-edge case use disc[v], not low[v], and only when v is still on the stack — a visited vertex that has already been popped belongs to a finished SCC and must not lower low[u]. Using low[v] still yields correct SCCs here, but the identical-looking articulation-point algorithm below genuinely breaks with that mistake.

Articulation points (cut vertices)

Articulation point — a vertex of a connected undirected graph whose removal (with its edges) disconnects the graph — the single point of failure in a network. A graph with no articulation point is biconnected.

Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 3-4, V = 5
Output: 1 3

Naive solution. Remove every vertex in turn and count the connected components of what is left (skipping the removed vertex). If the count goes above 1, the vertex is an articulation point. One DFS per vertex: O(V · (V + E)).

First idea (DFS tree, root only). Run a DFS and look at its tree. If the root has two or more DFS children, the root is an articulation point: the subtrees are separate branches that no back edge can connect (an undirected DFS tree has no cross edges, so an edge between two subtrees would have been a tree edge). The rule is only valid for the root — any other vertex can have several children that are still joined through back edges to its ancestors.

Tarjan's algorithm (low-link values). Give every vertex a discovery time disc[u] (the DFS counter when u is first visited) and a low value low[u]: the smallest discovery time reachable from u's subtree using tree edges plus at most one back edge. A non-root u is an articulation point iff some DFS child v has low[v] ≥ disc[u] — nothing in v's subtree climbs above u, so removing u strands that subtree.

Idea

low[u] starts as disc[u]. A back edge u – v to an already visited vertex (that is not the parent) lowers it to disc[v]; after returning from a child v, low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). The check low[v] >= disc[u] is made right after dfs(v) returns, when low[v] is final.

1
Discover
On entering u: disc[u] = low[u] = timer++, children = 0.
2
Tree edge
For an unvisited neighbour v: children++, dfs(v), then low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]). If u is not the root and low[v] >= disc[u], mark u.
3
Back edge
For a visited neighbour v that is not the parent: low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]).
4
Root rule
After the loop: if u is the root and children >= 2, mark u.
Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Pitfall

Two classic mistakes. (1) Applying the low[v] >= disc[u] test to the root: the root's disc is 0, so every child passes it and the root would always be reported — the root needs the children count instead. (2) Writing low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]) for a back edge: low[v] may already have been lowered through v's own back edges to vertices above u, which makes u look safe when it is not. For a back edge use disc[v].

Key point

The same disc/low arrays answer several questions at once: articulation points (low[v] >= disc[u]), bridges (low[v] > disc[u], next section) and, in a directed graph, strongly connected components (low[u] == disc[u]). Learn the DFS once and remember the three conditions.

Bridges (cut edges)

Bridge — an edge of a connected undirected graph whose removal disconnects the graph. Every bridge lies on no cycle; equivalently, an edge is a bridge exactly when it is not part of any cycle.

Example

Input: edges = 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 1-3, 3-4
Output: 1-3 3-4
Input: edges = 0-1, 1-2, 2-0, 2-3, 3-4, 4-2
Output: none

Idea

Same DFS, same disc and low, one character different. The tree edge u – v is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u]: nothing in v's subtree reaches u or anything above it, so the tree edge is the only way out. With >= a back edge landing exactly on u would still count as a cycle through u – v, which is why that case is an articulation point but not a bridge. There is no root special case for bridges.

Time O(V + E)Space O(V)
Articulation point uBridge u – v
Condition (tree edge u → v)low[v] >= disc[u]low[v] > disc[u]
Root special caseYes — >= 2 DFS childrenNone
Removing itDisconnects the graph; also removes its edgesDisconnects the graph; vertices stay
RelationBoth endpoints of a bridge are articulation points unless they have degree 1A graph can have articulation points but no bridges (graph 2 above)
Pitfall

With parallel edges the v != parent test is wrong for bridges — a doubled edge u = v is never a bridge, yet both copies are skipped as “the edge we came from”. Skip only the parent edge index (pass the index of the edge used to enter u), not every edge to the parent vertex. This matters for bridges more than for articulation points, because a double edge genuinely changes the answer.

Minimum spanning tree — Kruskal's algorithm

Minimum spanning tree (MST) — of a connected, undirected, weighted graph: a subset of V − 1 edges that connects every vertex (a spanning tree) with the smallest possible total weight. Laying cable between cities, clustering, approximating TSP — anything that asks for the cheapest way to connect everything.

Example

Input: edges above, V = 5
Output: MST edges 0-2 (1), 1-2 (2), 3-4 (2), 1-3 (5); total weight 10

Idea

Greedy on edges. Sort all edges by weight and take them in order, keeping an edge only if its two endpoints are not already connected — otherwise it would close a cycle. The cheapest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST (the cut property), and the first edge that joins two separate pieces is exactly that cheapest crossing edge. Stop after V − 1 edges.

1
Sort
All E edges by weight, ascending — O(E log E).
2
Initialise
mst = {}, total = 0, every vertex in its own set.
3
Scan
For each edge (u, v, w) in sorted order, while |mst| < V − 1: if u and v are in different sets, add the edge, total += w, and merge the two sets.
4
Return
total and the chosen edges.

Naive version (from the notes). Keep the partial MST as a separate graph and, for every candidate edge, run a DFS in it to see whether u can already reach v — if so, the edge would form a cycle. Correct, but each check costs O(V) and there are E of them: O(E · V).

Efficient version. The “are u and v already connected?” question is exactly what a disjoint set (union–find) answers in near-constant time: find(u) == find(v) means same component; union(u, v) merges two. With path compression (point every node on the find path straight at the root) and union by rank (hang the shorter tree under the taller) each operation is O(α(V)), effectively constant, so the sort dominates.

Time O(E log E) for the sort; the union–find work is O(E · α(V))Space O(V + E)
Pitfall

Forgetting the cycle check (just taking the V − 1 cheapest edges) is the classic wrong answer: here the three cheapest edges are 0-2, 1-2, 3-4 and the fourth cheapest, 0-1 (4), closes the triangle 0-1-2 — Kruskal must skip it and take 1-3 (5). Also: if the graph is disconnected, fewer than V − 1 edges get chosen and the result is a minimum spanning forest, not a tree — check the count.

Key point

Kruskal works on the plain edge list — no adjacency list needed — and is the natural choice when the edges are already sorted or arrive one at a time. Because it processes edges globally rather than growing from a vertex, it also handles disconnected graphs gracefully.

Minimum spanning tree — Prim's algorithm

Idea

Greedy on vertices. Grow the tree from one start vertex: at every step add the cheapest edge that leaves the tree (one endpoint inside, one outside). That edge crosses the cut between the tree and the rest, so by the cut property it belongs to an MST. It is Dijkstra with a different key: the edge weight alone instead of the distance from the source.

Example

Input: edges above, start = 0
Output: MST edges 0-2 (1), 2-1 (2), 1-3 (5), 3-4 (2); total weight 10 — the same tree Kruskal found, grown in a different order

1
Initialise
inMST[v] = false for all v; push (0, start, −1) into a min-heap keyed by weight.
2
Extract-min
Pop (w, v, from). If v is already in the tree, skip (a stale entry).
3
Add
Mark inMST[v]; if from != −1 record the edge from – v and total += w.
4
Push neighbours
For every edge v – x with weight w' where x is not in the tree: push (w', x, v).
Time O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap; O(V²) with an array scanSpace O(V + E)
Pitfall

Prim's key is the weight of the single edge into the tree, not the accumulated distance from the start — copy Dijkstra's d + w by habit and you get a shortest-path tree, which is generally not a minimum spanning tree. On this graph the two happen to coincide (same four edges, total 10); on the triangle 0-1 (2), 1-2 (2), 0-2 (3) the MST is {0-1, 1-2} with weight 4 while Dijkstra's tree from 0 is {0-1, 0-2} with weight 5. Prim also assumes a connected graph: started from one vertex it never reaches another component.

Key point

Both are greedy and both are correct because of the cut property: for any partition of the vertices into two sets, the cheapest edge crossing the partition is in some MST. Kruskal applies it to the cut between the two components an edge joins; Prim applies it to the cut between the tree and everything else.

Two questions sort almost every graph problem: directed or undirected? and weighted or not? Interview Q&A

BFS or DFS — how do you decide?

BFS when distance from the source matters: shortest path in an unweighted graph, nearest neighbour, anything level by level. DFS when the structure matters: cycle detection, topological order, strongly connected components, articulation points, backtracking through a state space. Both are O(V + E); BFS uses O(width) memory for the frontier, DFS O(depth) for the recursion stack (and recursion can overflow on long paths — use an explicit stack for big inputs).

Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edge weights?

Dijkstra settles the closest unsettled vertex and assumes its distance is final, because with non-negative weights any other route must pass through a farther vertex and can only get longer. A negative edge breaks that assumption: a longer-looking route can end up shorter once it takes the negative edge, so an already settled vertex would need to be improved. Example: 0→1 (2), 0→2 (5), 2→1 (−4) — Dijkstra settles 1 at distance 2, but the true distance is 1. Use Bellman–Ford, or a single topological pass if the graph is a DAG.

Kahn's algorithm or DFS for topological sort?

Both are O(V + E) and both give a valid order. Kahn's (indegree + queue) is iterative, detects cycles automatically (fewer than V vertices output) and, with a min-heap in place of the queue, gives the lexicographically smallest order — which is why it is usually preferred in interviews. The DFS version (reverse finish order) is shorter to write and is the same post-order that Kosaraju's SCC algorithm uses, but it silently produces garbage on a cyclic graph unless you add the onStack check.

Adjacency list or adjacency matrix — which do you choose and why?

Default to the adjacency list: Θ(V + E) memory and Θ(degree) to scan a vertex's neighbours, so every traversal is Θ(V + E). Real graphs are sparse — a social network with a billion users does not have 10^18 friendships — and a matrix would need Θ(V²) space just to store zeros. Pick the matrix when the graph is dense (E ≈ V²), when O(1) “is there an edge u – v?” lookups dominate, or when the algorithm is matrix-shaped (Floyd–Warshall, Prim's O(V²) version).

Kruskal or Prim — which would you use?

Both are greedy, both are correct by the cut property, and both give an MST of the same weight. Kruskal sorts the edge list and uses union–find: O(E log E), works straight from an edge list, handles disconnected graphs (it returns a spanning forest) — the choice for sparse graphs or when edges are already sorted. Prim grows one tree with a heap: O((V + E) log V), or O(V²) with a plain array scan, which beats Kruskal on dense graphs and adjacency-matrix input. In practice: sparse → Kruskal, dense → Prim.

What does the low-link value mean, and what are the three conditions built on it?

disc[u] is the DFS counter when u is discovered; low[u] is the smallest disc that u's subtree can reach using tree edges plus at most one back edge. It measures how far up the DFS tree a subtree can climb without using its parent edge. Three tests follow from it, all O(V + E) in one DFS: a tree edge u – v is a bridge when low[v] > disc[u] (the subtree cannot climb to u or above); a non-root u is an articulation point when low[v] >= disc[u] for some child v (the subtree reaches u at best — removing u strands it; the root instead needs two or more DFS children); and in a directed graph u is the root of an SCC when low[u] == disc[u], at which point the stack above u is popped as one component.
